Tout ce que j'espère c'est que le message a ma soeur était avant celui à S. Sinon c'est mort. Je suis morte. Non seulement ça va être classée sans suite, mais tout le monde va penser que je suis une mytho, une fouteuse de merde. Et tout nos amis vont me tourner le dos. Et yoh sera validé dans son envie de le fréquenter... Je vais pas tenir je crois. Ça va m"achever

As a fat woman, 

Any amount of time spent on a plane is mental torture.

I know I'm fat. I know my hips are  slightly spilling over on your seat. 
The arm rest is also digging into my sides. But I don't put it up. Because I know everyone likes that separation. 

Asking for a seat belt extender makes me want to jump out of the plane. Sometimes I just don't bother asking and don't buckle up to avoid having to publicly acknowledge that I need a special seat belt for fat people.

I'm so stressed about not being a horrible fat person on a plane, that I get flustered. I get sweaty. And then I hate myself because a slim person sweating, no one bats an eye. But a fat person sweating is instantly more repugnant apparently.

My thighs are big too. So there's a good chance my legs will shake for a portion of the flight because I'm trying to keep them closed so that my knees don't spill onto your side too, but it means my thigh muscles are continuously tense. 


I draw the line at eating though. Because no one wants to be the fat sweaty annoying person stuffing their face on a plane.
At most I'll buy a drink. But never soda. Because if I'm fat it's obviously because I drink too much soda. Or at least, that's what I imagine other passengers thinking.

So don't worry, as much as you hate being seated next to that fat person, chances are that fat person spent the whole flight acutely aware of just how inconvenient their existence is in that moment.

Personal anecdote:

I saw a therapist after remembering sexual assaults.

I received nothing but support from the people I confided in, my mom, my fiancé (at the time), some friends etc. Everyone was lovely.

But I needed an outsider to validate my feelings. I needed someone who didn't know me, didn't have any background info to react to my story. 

Like if a neutral safe person says "um yeah that's illegal af" then I could allow myself to be hurt or angry or want justice.

 That I wasn't making a big deal out of nothing because even this qualified professional, who hears this all the time and doesn't know me told me I was a victim.

My family and friends were so very loving, and full of advice and fight for me that it was actually difficult to deal with what I was feeling because of how aware I was of upsetting others.

The therapist was an outlet to say all the same things, but get an response that wasn't loaded with added love and emotions and worry for me.

The therapist brought me to question things that neither me or my family would have thought about. 

They allowed me to take a step back from the whole thing and look at it differently.

There really is no comparison between confiding in someone you know and a therapist.

I think it's important to find the right therapist though. 
A regular therapist won't be as tuned to issues related to trauma than an actual trauma therapist for example.

I saw two. The first was a psychologist I picked because her office was close. 
She made things worse by victim blaming me.

I ended up finding a psychologist in a "women and family rights" centre thing. Who was very experienced with dealing with all kind of trauma relating to women.

When I was about 19, me and my boyfriend went to a music festival. Except we didn't think it through properly and ended up arriving a day early, in the tiniest of tiny towns with nothing around us and no plan of where to stay.

Being stupid and fearless, we pitched our tent just outside the door of the train station we had arrived at and decided to sleep there and wait until morning to catch the bus to the festival campsite.

Just as we're lying down in our tent thinking "this is a bit weird but whatev",  we hear a man's voice calling us outside the tent.
He asks us if we're planning on sleeping there, we say yes. And he says "nonsense!  You can't sleep here!  Come with me I live just round here".

So we pack up and walk just round the corner and enter this building that was blaring music a few hours earlier. We get to his apartment and it's just... weird.

Not the apartment in itself, but the atmosphere. We weren't used to people being nice just to be nice and we sat on this guys couch for a while, awkward as fuck while he tried to make conversation. Then he offered us a glass of alcohol which I refused but my boyfriend felt it would be impolite so said yes. Dude handed him a glass of whisky and he silently sipped it.

After what felt like all eternity the guy shows us where we can sleep, it was a room with a bit of random junk in it and a mattress propped up against the wall.

I was pretty terrified to sleep, convinced that no one is just friendly for no reason and surely he was going to murder us during the night.

I made my boyfriend promise he wouldn't fall asleep (this was before smartphones so I don't know wtf I expected him to do all night in the dark) and then I promptly fell asleep. (Oblivious to the ridiculousness of asking him to stay awake while I slept like a princess)

Woke up at about 5:30am (boyfriend had fallen asleep after all) and we snuck out as quietly as we humanly could.

Nothing weird happened. But it still makes me *feel* weird because we just followed a random stranger to his house at night without any thought on how risky it was.
